questions.q: Why does a designer need to consider the industrial and commercial practices that will be used during manufacturing?
options: To ensure the product will sell
To gain access to cheaper resources
To increase the product's rate of production
To produce products that meet market needs
questions.explanation: Understanding industrial and commercial manufacturing practices lets a designer plan for efficient mass production and a higher rate of production. The other options are commercial outcomes that depend on, but are not the direct reason for, considering these practices.

questions.q: Outcome H6.1 relates four industrial and commercial practices to your major design project. Which set names all four (the hook SPPC)?
options: Sketching, prototyping, packaging, costing
Safe work practices, production techniques, process selection, collaborative design teams
Sourcing materials, planning, presentation, communication
Sustainability, profit, productivity, customer service
questions.explanation: The syllabus names safe work practices using selected resources, production techniques, the selection of processes appropriate to the need, and collaborative designing and design teams — held with the hook SPPC. These are the four lenses for comparing your work to industry.

questions.q: What is the key move that earns H6.1 marks when relating an industrial practice to your own production?
options: Copy the factory's scale and equipment as closely as your budget allows
Adapt the principle of the industrial practice to your own scale, not copy the scale itself
Contrast how many units industry makes versus how many you made
List every machine a factory would use to make your product
questions.explanation: You adapt the principle of an industrial practice to your project — for example using a hand jig to get the same repeatability a factory achieves with a CNC machine. Simply contrasting scale ('they make millions, I made one') is description, not the relating-and-justifying H6.1 wants.

questions.q: Which of the following options best describes the features of a collaborative design team?
options: Leader directed, common skills among the group, responsive to feedback
Leader directed, various fields of professional expertise, responsive to feedback
Shared understanding of the project, common skills among the team, cooperative decision-making process
Shared understanding of the project, various fields of professional expertise, cooperative decision-making process
questions.explanation: A collaborative team shares a common understanding of the project, brings together varied fields of expertise, and makes decisions cooperatively rather than being directed by a single leader. Option D captures all three features.

questions.q: A design team works best when
options: tasks are allocated to individuals based on expertise.
the designer’s work flow is structured and organised.
design teams work in direct competition with each other.
team members always work independently towards a goal.
questions.explanation: Effective collaborative design teams allocate tasks according to each member's expertise so the right skills are applied to each part of the project. Constant competition or working independently undermines the cooperation that makes a team productive.

questions.q: When you relate your own production to industry, what stays the same and what differs?
options: The design process differs entirely; only the marketing is shared
The design process and underlying principles are the same; scale, resources and formality differ
Everything is the same because a school workshop is just a small factory
The materials are identical; only the cost differs
questions.explanation: Across the settings (DCIC: domestic, community, industrial, commercial) and scales (JBM: job, batch, mass) from module two, the design process and principles such as repeatability and quality control are shared. What differs is scale, resources and the level of formality — your MDP is usually one-off, job production while industry mass-produces.

questions.q: From memory: what four industrial and commercial practices does the syllabus relate to the MDP, and what is the key to relating them to your own work?
keyPoints: The four practices (SPPC): Safe work practices using selected resources, Production techniques, Process selection appropriate to the need, and Collaborative designing and design teams.
The key is to adapt the principle of an industrial practice to your own scale — not to copy the scale itself.
Example: use a hand jig or template to achieve the repeatability a factory gets from a CNC machine.
questions.explanation: If you recalled SPPC and 'adapt the principle, not the scale', grade yourself Good or Easy. The comparison, justified, is the whole skill of H6.1.

questions.q: In your own words, map two industrial practices to how you could adapt each in a one-off school MDP, naming the principle behind each.
keyPoints: Industrial CNC machining for repeatable parts → a hand jig or template for hand-made repeatability (principle: repeatability/precision).
Industrial quality-control sampling → checking each component against your success criteria (principle: quality control).
Industrial spray-finishing on a line → careful hand-finishing to the same standard (principle: finish), or division of labour → sequencing your own tasks efficiently (principle: efficiency).
questions.explanation: Each row is the same principle — repeatability, quality, efficiency, finish — achieved at your scale. Naming that principle is what justifies your process by reference to professional practice.

questions.q: Relate a production technique used in industrial settings to your major design project. (5 marks)
questions.modelAnswer: In industrial furniture manufacturing, jigs and computer-controlled machinery are used to ensure that every component is produced identically and accurately and that assembly is fast and consistent — the principle being repeatability and precision at high volume. In my major design project, working as a one-off in a school setting, I related this practice by designing and making a simple drilling jig for my chair legs. Although my scale was far smaller and the jig was hand-made rather than computer-controlled, it applied the same principle: it ensured all four legs were drilled identically, giving consistent, accurate assembly I could not have achieved reliably by hand. I therefore justified my process by reference to the industrial practice, adapting its principle of repeatability to my scale and resources.

criteria.descriptor: Names a specific industrial production technique and explains its underlying principle (e.g. jigs/CNC for repeatability and precision).
Relates the technique to a specific adaptation in the student's own MDP at their scale.
Justifies the process by reference to the industrial principle; a surface scale-contrast caps low.

questions.explanation: The marker rewards naming the practice, explaining its principle, relating it to a concrete adaptation in your project, and justifying the choice — not merely contrasting scale.

questions.q: To what extent have technological advancements in production techniques influenced changes in design? Support your answer with examples.
questions.modelAnswer: Technological advancements in modern production techniques give designers greater versatility in how materials can be combined, formed, shaped and labelled, allowing products to meet a broader range of social demands. For example, equipment that produces rippled paper has let designers create the insulating, rigid take-away coffee cup through a simple, cost-effective, mass-produced process. Advancements in laser cutting and automated production have also changed traditional techniques, shifting products toward design for assembly — flat-pack products reduce production and consumer costs and stimulate further design refinement. However, these techniques often require expensive equipment, staff training and additional resources, so in some cases they have not influenced design changes as much or as quickly as they could have. Overall, technological advancements have influenced design changes to a large extent.

criteria.descriptor: Makes the relationship evident why technological advancements in production techniques have influenced changes in design; provides relevant examples
Provides characteristics and features of technological advancements in production techniques that have influenced changes in design; provides examples
Indicates the main features of technological advancements in production techniques that have influenced changes in design; provides example(s)
Demonstrates some understanding of technological advancements in production techniques and/or changes in design

questions.explanation: This is a real HSC extended-response question. The episode's process-selection theme (e.g. the Flow Hive scaling to injection moulding) is exactly this relationship between production techniques and design choices.
